idiom_name: hand-rolled session table over OpenSSL RAND_bytes
implementation_notes: ISO C has no session abstraction, so the manager is explicit: a session table keyed by a 256-bit token from OpenSSL's CSPRNG (RAND_bytes), a record holding principal, attributes, creation and last-use timestamps plus idle/absolute expiry, a synchronised lookup (mutex or RW-lock; a shared Redis table once several processes serve users) and constant-time comparison of the presented token. The cookie is written by hand with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite attributes. The classic Session Manager, Session Store and transport roles therefore stay hand-written; OpenSSL's man page warns that the CSPRNG refuses to produce output when entropy is unavailable rather than returning weak bytes, so the return value must be checked, and OWASP's property checklist is what the implementation must satisfy.
code_sketch:
unsigned char id[32];
if (RAND_bytes(id, sizeof id) != 1) return -1;      /* CSPRNG, checked      */
session *s = store_create(store, id, now);          /* state server-side    */
session_touch(s, now);                              /* idle + absolute      */
res_set_cookie(res, "sid", to_hex(id),              /* HttpOnly; Secure;    */
               COOKIE_HTTPONLY | COOKIE_SECURE | COOKIE_SAMESITE_STRICT);
store_delete(store, id);                            /* logout: revoke now   */
pitfalls: A hash table without a lock, or a process-local table behind several workers, either corrupts under concurrency or silently splits sessions; synchronise and move to a shared store when there is more than one process.
Expiry must be swept, not only checked on lookup, or the table leaks one entry per abandoned session; cap the table and evict.
Comparing tokens with memcmp leaks timing; compare in constant time and never log or format the raw token.
Forgetting HttpOnly and Secure on the Set-Cookie header, or accepting the token from a query parameter, reopens fixation and theft.
